speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Minister for Transport in light of industry reports that the global supply chain congestion is easing and normalising (a) what percentage of its capacity is Singapore’s seaport presently operating at; (b) what will the impact of a "normalisation" of global supply chains have on our seaport; and (c) whether the Ministry needs to scale up or augment our seaport’s capacity to prepare for the expected change in the shipping landscape over the next year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am very concerned because of the recent report in Bloomberg which shared that the New York Federal Reserve's Global Supply Chain Pressure Index fell for a fifth straight month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is that there could be a potential scenario where we could see an untangling of transport snarls which are happening just as fast as the system knotted up previously, last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned that we have enough capacity and resources to potentially absorb some increase in activity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But will there be a possible scenario in 2023, where the activity picks up substantially, despite some risk of economic slowdown globally?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It could potentially pick up and do we have enough manpower, resources and also the fact that we are in the transition of shifting to Tuas from our current location?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The maritime and shipping industry is one that goes through up cycles and down cycles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, shipping lines and port operators are used to dealing with ups and downs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Importantly, one of the key drivers of port container volume is global trade and supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are some signs of certain sectors like manufacturing, for example, slowing down because of what is happening in different parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, while some of the factors may point towards increases in trade volumes, there are also other factors that point in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Regardless of whether it is up cycle or down cycle or an increase in volume or a decrease in volume, what is most critical is this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We maintain very strong tripartite partnerships among employers, unions and Government agencies to always look at how we can maintain our port competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is, of course, partly driven by our capabilities like the skills of our workers and the technology we deploy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, these are all different ways to amplify the impact of our workforce to improve productivity and to improve our port competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second very important factor when it comes to competitiveness for port operations is connectivity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why we served as a catch-up port during the pandemic because people who got delayed elsewhere come to Singapore to rearrange their cargoes and use us as a catch-up port to make up for lost time.
